_comment: The one shared material palette for every procedurally generated Machine.
Dieselpunk: 1920s-40s heavy industry. Cast iron, welded steel, olive drab
paint over red-oxide primer, oiled hydraulics, soot and grime. Brass and
copper appear only as small fittings - this is not Victorian steampunk, and
a machine that reads as brass has gone wrong.
Declared here rather than in the generator so that visual consistency is a
fact a test can check: the asset suite asserts that every generated .glb
uses materials from this file and nothing else, and that the numbers match.
base_color is linear RGBA, which is what both Blender's Principled BSDF and
glTF's baseColorFactor take, so the value survives export unchanged.
`texture` names a map in assets/generated/textures, generated on this
machine by tools/aigen. `texture_scale_m` is how many metres across one
tile of it covers on a Machine: the meshes are UV'd at world scale, one UV
unit to the metre, so this number is the only thing that sets texture
density, and a Machine that is made bigger does not stretch its surface.
An entry with no `texture` is painted colour only, on purpose - a gauge
bezel is 11 cm across and a sight glass 7 cm, so a 1024x1024 map on them
would cost VRAM to render a coloured dot. poured_concrete is in the
generated set and is deliberately not here: it is the Map's floor, not a
surface any Machine wears.
Where a material has a texture, THE TEXTURE CARRIES THE COLOUR. The set was
generated per surface - cast iron is iron-coloured, olive drab is olive -
so multiplying it by base_color as well would square an already dark value
and render every Machine as a black box with a sheen. base_color stays the
authority for the untextured entries, for the glTF baseColorFactor the asset
suite checks, and as the flat fallback.
`texture_tint` is what each map is multiplied by, and it is the knob that
brings the generated set back to this palette's values. The maps were made
to be lit as photographs and come out a stop or two brighter and more
saturated than interwar machinery ever looked; a tint near 0.5 grey darkens
a surface without flattening the relief, which multiplying by base_color
(0.055 for cast iron) would do. Hazard striping is the other kind of tint:
the set has no yellow surface, so the grey tread plate is pushed past 1.0
into yellow. Default is white.
The four dielectric entries land ABOVE their own base_color and the three
metals do not - OliveDrab 1.78x, OxideRed 1.64x, BeltRubber 2.22x, Soot
2.95x, against CastIron 0.87, WeldedSteel 1.01, OiledSteel 0.94. That is an
accident rather than a decision: #80 measured it, and the likeliest story is
that whoever tuned this column tuned it while looking at metal. #82 then
corrected all four, rendered the yard, a line, a Belt from above and the
Nest, and measured the result - and it is KEPT, deliberately, for three
reasons a later reader should have rather than rediscover.
It desaturates as much as it darkens. A dielectric's specular is about 4%
white and does not scale with albedo, so lowering albedo raises the
specular's share: the Smelter's oxide band went to 0.80x luminance and
0.81x saturation together, and a rust band became a pale salmon one.
OxideRed's job is primer showing through, and a desaturated pink is not
primer.
It re-ranks the Factory's colours. HazardYellow is the exemption above and
is the one entry a correction leaves alone, so correcting the other four
makes the safety striping 1.39x louder against the olive beside it -
measured - and the stripes become the loudest thing a player sees.
And it buys almost nothing. These four are 0.7% to 5.6% of the screen in
every vantage measured, so the frame-wide median moved by about 0.3% while
every Machine, every Belt deck and all of #73's cargo changed. The ratios
are wrong and correcting them costs more than the error. If the world is
ever too bright or too dark the lever is WorldView._sync_scenery; what this
column owns is the relation between entries, not the level of the world.
The trap that leaves behind is a body rather than an entry. A surface where
the overshoot compounds with area and orientation renders far above
everything near it - the Nest's raked tiers did, at 6.4x the ground, which
is what #80 was. The guard is #80's rule rather than this number: render a
new body at the range a player meets it, from both vantages, and measure it
against its neighbours.

materials.name: CastIron
materials._use: Machine bodies, frames, heavy castings. The default surface.

materials.name: WeldedSteel
materials._use: Plate panels, brackets, catwalks, bolted flanges.

materials.name: OliveDrab
materials._use: Painted housings and cowlings. The silhouette colour.

materials.name: OxideRed
materials._use: Primer showing through where paint has gone, and inner frames.

materials.name: OiledSteel
materials._use: Hydraulic rams, piston rods, shafts. Wet-looking, not shiny.

materials.name: DullBrass
materials._use: Gauge bezels and small fittings only. Used sparingly on purpose.

materials.name: Soot
materials._use: Chimney mouths, firebox interiors, grime in recesses.

materials.name: HazardYellow
materials._use: Port collars and edge stripes. Reads a port at a glance.
